chunks: We were told by my father, may Allah grant him mercy, that he said: We were told by Sa'd bin Abdullah, that he said: We were told by Muhammad bin Isa bin Ubaid, from Ubaidullah bin Abdullah al-Dahqan, from Darust bin Abi Mansur al-Wasiti, from Ibrahim bin Abdul-Hamid, from Abu'l-Hasan, peace be upon him, who said:

The Messenger of Allah, Allah’s blessings be upon him and his Family, entered the Mosque, and a group of people were circling around a man, so he said: What is this? They said: A great scholar, O Allah’s Messenger. Then he said: And what great scholar (is he)? They said: The most knowledgeable among the people about the lineages of the Arabs, their incidents, the days of the Jahiliya and poetry. Then he, Allah’s blessings be upon him and his Family, said: That is a knowledge that does not harm the one who is ignorant of it, nor does it benefit the one who knows it.

key_terms.أَيَّامُ الْجَاهِلِيَّةِ: The days of the pre-Islamic era

ai.seo_question: What kind of knowledge does not benefit a person spiritually according to the Prophet?
ai.summary: In this hadith from Shaykh al-Saduq’s *Ma'ani al-Akhbar*, the Prophet (SAW) distinguishes between utilitarian worldly knowledge (*al-'ilm al-'amali*) and spiritually transformative knowledge (*al-'ilm al-nafi'*). This classification underscores the Shia scholarly emphasis that mastery of genealogy and pre-Islamic poetry, while culturally significant, lacks the capacity to elevate one's soul or bring one closer to God, thereby serving as a critique of knowledge pursued for status rather than divine proximity.
